# How to Manage Cash Flow During Peak Trading Periods


- by[Katie Nelson](https://www.lightspeedhq.com/blog/author/katie-nelson/)
- 2026-11-26


minute read


Share Post


-
-
-


A busy holiday season can bring a welcome lift in sales, but in the weeks before the rush hits, your cash flow might feel the squeeze. You may need to pay suppliers, bring on seasonal staff or launch a campaign weeks before customers start buying.


That timing gap is one reason a retailer can be busy and still feel pressure on day-to-day cash. Therefore, it’s important to understand when money is expected to come in and go out, decide which investments matter most and keep checking the plan as the season unfolds.


In this article, we’ll explore how to manage cash flow during peak trading periods—from forecasting and inventory decisions to payments and funding options.


## **Why can peak trading put pressure on retail cash flow?**


Peak season concentrates activity. You might order more inventory, schedule extra shifts, increase shipping supplies and spend more on marketing. Those costs can arrive before the products sell or before revenue reaches your account.


A large order can also tie up cash that you may need for rent, payroll, utilities or an unexpected repair. Meanwhile, a promotion may bring in more orders but reduce your margin if the discount is too deep or the products don’t sell as planned.


There’s another distinction worth keeping in mind: sales, profit and cash aren’t the same thing. A sale contributes to revenue, but cash flow depends on when money is collected and when expenses are paid. Returns, payment processing timelines and supplier terms can all affect that timing.


That doesn’t mean a strong season has to create a cash crunch. It means your plan needs to account for the calendar—not just the sales target.


## **How can you forecast cash needs before the rush?**


A useful forecast doesn’t need to predict the season perfectly, but it should make upcoming commitments visible early enough for you to respond.


### **Start with last season’s numbers—and update them**


Review sales by week, product, channel and location. Look at what sold quickly, what stayed on the shelf, when returns picked up and which promotions helped move inventory. Compare those patterns with what’s happening now: current stock levels, supplier lead times, planned events and changes in how customers shop.


Use last year as a reference, not a promise. A product that sold well last season may not perform the same way this year, so check recent demand before placing a large reorder.


### **Map expected inflows and outflows by week**


Create a simple calendar for the weeks leading up to and during your busiest period. Add expected sales and the costs you know are coming. Include supplier deposits and balances, payroll, rent, shipping, marketing, taxes and regular operating expenses.


Be specific about timing. “Inventory: $X” is less useful than noting when a deposit is due, when the remaining balance is due and when you expect to start selling those products. The same goes for payment deposits: check the settlement schedule that applies to your business rather than assuming every sale will be available immediately.


The calendar can help you spot a tight week before it arrives—even if the full-season forecast looks healthy. It also helps protect the cash you need to keep regular operations running.


### **Build a base case and a slower-sales case**


Write down what you expect to happen, then consider what changes if sales come in below plan or a delivery arrives late. Which purchases can be staged? Which costs are already committed? What would you pause first without affecting customer service or essential operations?


Check the forecast at least weekly during peak trading. Compare it with actual sales, expenses and deposits, then adjust the plan. A forecast is most useful when it changes as the business does.

## **How should you prioritize inventory, staffing and marketing?**


When several costs compete for the same cash, start with the decision’s timing, evidence and likely impact on the business. Ask what needs to happen before the rush, what can wait and what will help customers find or buy the products they want.


### **Buy inventory with demand and cash timing in mind**


Use sales history, current stock, margins and supplier lead times to decide what to reorder. Prioritize products with a clear role in your seasonal assortment and a realistic chance of selling through. Keep an eye on slow-moving stock too; ordering more of it can tie up cash without improving availability where it matters.


If your supplier allows it, ask whether an order can be split into smaller deliveries or staged payments. That may help match purchasing decisions more closely to demand. Weigh any change against the supplier’s terms, delivery costs and the risk of missing sales if stock runs short.


If you sell in more than one channel or location, review stock across the business before ordering. Accurate, shared inventory information can help you see what’s available and where it’s needed.


### **Schedule labor around expected demand**


Use sales patterns, promotions and local events to estimate when you’ll need more coverage. Plan for the work behind the sale as well as the transaction itself: receiving stock, restocking shelves, packing online orders, handling pickup and processing returns.


Give new and returning staff time to learn the workflows they’ll use most. Practice common scenarios before the busiest shifts, including exchanges, discounts, gift cards and finding an item at another location. Clear processes can make it easier for the team to serve shoppers when the store is busy.


### **Set a measurable budget for promotions**


Choose a goal before you launch a campaign. Are you trying to introduce a product, bring shoppers into the store or sell through a particular category? Decide what you’ll track and when you’ll review the results.


A planned review point gives you a chance to adjust a promotion if it isn’t delivering the response you expected. It can also help you avoid committing the full seasonal marketing budget before you know what’s working.


## **What operational and payment improvements can support cash flow?**


Cash-flow planning is easier when you can see what sold, what was refunded and what has been deposited. During a busy period, checking that information regularly can help you respond to changes sooner than if you wait until month-end.


### **Make sales and payment information easier to reconcile**


Set a regular time to compare sales reports with payment deposits, fees and refunds. If information lives in separate systems, decide who will bring it together and how often. Make sure unusual differences are followed up while the transaction is still easy to trace.


When payment records connect with sales activity, there may be fewer details to match by hand. That can make it easier to review trading activity and spot questions that need attention. The benefit is clearer information—not a guarantee that cash will arrive sooner or that every reconciliation issue will disappear.

### **Reduce avoidable friction at checkout and across channels**


Walk through a typical sale from start to finish. Check that devices are working, product information is current and staff know how to handle common returns, discounts and payment questions. If shoppers can buy online and in store, review how your team checks availability, handles pickup and updates inventory.


A short pre-season test can surface small issues before they become repeated workarounds. Ask staff where they lose time, which steps get repeated and what tends to go wrong at checkout. Then focus on the fixes that matter most to both the customer experience and the team’s ability to serve shoppers.


### **Track a short list of indicators**


You don’t need a complicated dashboard to keep an eye on the season. Choose a few useful measures and review them on a regular schedule:


- Cash available and upcoming payments


- Sales compared with your forecast


- Inventory sell-through and stockouts


- Returns and refunds


- Payment deposits and fees


Assign someone to update the numbers and note what action you’ll take if results move away from plan. A short, consistent review can be more useful than a long list of metrics no one has time to act on.


## **What can you do when a planned investment exceeds available cash?**


Start by revisiting the investment. Can you stage the purchase, adjust its timing or reduce its scope without creating a bigger operational problem? Compare the full cost with the expected benefit and consider how long it may take for the investment to support sales.


If you still need more working capital, compare the options available to your business. Savings, supplier terms, lines of credit, business loans and sales-based funding (like a merchant cash advance) all work differently. Look at the total cost, how payments are calculated, when they’re due and how they could affect available cash flow for future expenses. Consider getting qualified financial or accounting advice if you need help evaluating an option.

## **A peak-season cash-flow checklist**


Before the rush:


- Review last season’s sales, returns and inventory performance.


- Build a weekly forecast of expected sales and expenses.


- Mark the weeks when major supplier, payroll or marketing costs are due.


- Prioritize inventory using current stock, demand and lead times.


- Plan staffing and train the team on busy-period workflows.


- Set a budget and review point for seasonal promotions.


- Test checkout, returns, payment and reporting processes.


During the rush:


- Compare actual sales and expenses with the forecast each week.


- Review deposits, fees and refunds regularly.


- Update inventory and staffing plans as demand changes.


- Revisit discretionary spending before committing more cash.


## **A clearer plan can help you make better seasonal decisions**


Peak trading will always involve some uncertainty. A weekly forecast, clear priorities and regular payment reviews can help you see what’s changing and decide what to do next. Start with the numbers you have, update them as the season unfolds and protect the cash your business needs to keep operating.
